# `record` data validation

Data validation in C# `record` types is an important topic. Let me walk you through your options, from simple to advanced.


## Overview of Validation Approaches


```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│           Record Validation Strategies                  │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                         │
│  1. Constructor Validation (Primary Constructor)        │
│     ├─ Validate in constructor body                     │
│     └─ Throw exceptions for invalid data                │
│                                                         │
│  2. Property Init Validation                            │
│     ├─ Validate in init accessors                       │
│     └─ Control during object initialization             │
│                                                         │
│  3. Data Annotations                                    │
│     ├─ Declarative attributes                           │
│     └─ Framework integration (ASP.NET, EF Core)         │
│                                                         │
│  4. FluentValidation Library                            │
│     ├─ Separate validation rules                        │
│     └─ Complex scenarios                                │
│                                                         │
│  5. Factory Methods / Smart Constructors                │
│     ├─ Return Result<T> or validation result            │
│     └─ Avoid exceptions for business logic              │
│                                                         │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```


## Constructor Validation (Simplest Approach)


Validate directly in the primary constructor - similar to how you'd do it in Dart or Python class constructors:

```csharp
// Basic validation in primary constructor
public record Patient(string Name, int Age, string HospitalNumber)
{
    public Patient(string Name, int Age, string HospitalNumber) : this(Name, Age, HospitalNumber)
    {
        // Validate Name
        if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(Name))
            throw new ArgumentException("Patient name cannot be empty", nameof(Name));
        
        // Validate Age
        if (Age < 0 || Age > 150)
            throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(Age), "Age must be between 0 and 150");
        
        // Validate Hospital Number format
        if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(HospitalNumber) || HospitalNumber.Length < 6)
            throw new ArgumentException("Invalid hospital number format", nameof(HospitalNumber));
    }
}

// Usage
try
{
    var patient = new Patient("John Doe", 45, "RM123456");
    var invalidPatient = new Patient("", -5, "123"); // Throws exception
}
catch (ArgumentException ex)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"Validation failed: {ex.Message}");
}
```


## Property Init Validation


For records with explicit properties, you can validate in `init` accessors:

```csharp
public record DicomStudy
{
    private string _studyInstanceUID;
    private DateTime _studyDate;
    
    public string StudyInstanceUID
    {
        get => _studyInstanceUID;
        init
        {
            if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(value))
                throw new ArgumentException("StudyInstanceUID cannot be empty");
            
            // Validate DICOM UID format (simplified)
            if (!value.Contains('.'))
                throw new ArgumentException("Invalid DICOM UID format");
            
            _studyInstanceUID = value;
        }
    }
    
    public DateTime StudyDate
    {
        get => _studyDate;
        init
        {
            if (value > DateTime.Now)
                throw new ArgumentException("Study date cannot be in the future");
            
            if (value < new DateTime(1900, 1, 1))
                throw new ArgumentException("Study date is too old");
            
            _studyInstanceUID = value;
        }
    }
    
    public string Modality { get; init; }
}

// Usage
var study = new DicomStudy
{
    StudyInstanceUID = "1.2.840.113619.2.55.3.123456",
    StudyDate = DateTime.Now.AddDays(-1),
    Modality = "CT"
};
```


## Data Annotations (Declarative Validation)


Use attributes from `System.ComponentModel.DataAnnotations` - very useful for ASP.NET Core APIs:

```csharp
using System.ComponentModel.DataAnnotations;

public record RadiologyReport
{
    [Required(ErrorMessage = "Accession number is required")]
    [StringLength(20, MinimumLength = 6, ErrorMessage = "Accession number must be 6-20 characters")]
    public string AccessionNumber { get; init; }
    
    [Required]
    [Range(1, 100, ErrorMessage = "Patient age must be between 1 and 100")]
    public int PatientAge { get; init; }
    
    [Required]
    [RegularExpression(@"^[A-Z]{2}\d{6}$", ErrorMessage = "Invalid HN format (expected: XX123456)")]
    public string HN { get; init; }
    
    [EmailAddress(ErrorMessage = "Invalid email format")]
    public string? RadiologistEmail { get; init; }
    
    [StringLength(5000, ErrorMessage = "Report findings cannot exceed 5000 characters")]
    public string Findings { get; init; }
}

// You need to manually validate (or use ASP.NET which does it automatically)
using System.ComponentModel.DataAnnotations;

public static class RecordValidator
{
    public static (bool IsValid, List<string> Errors) Validate<T>(T record)
    {
        var context = new ValidationContext(record);
        var results = new List<ValidationResult>();
        
        bool isValid = Validator.TryValidateObject(record, context, results, validateAllProperties: true);
        
        var errors = results.Select(r => r.ErrorMessage ?? "Unknown error").ToList();
        return (isValid, errors);
    }
}

// Usage
var report = new RadiologyReport
{
    AccessionNumber = "RM12",  // Too short
    PatientAge = 150,  // Out of range
    HN = "invalid",    // Wrong format
    Findings = "Normal chest X-ray"
};

var (isValid, errors) = RecordValidator.Validate(report);
if (!isValid)
{
    Console.WriteLine("Validation errors:");
    errors.ForEach(e => Console.WriteLine($"  - {e}"));
}
```


## FluentValidation Library (Advanced)


For complex validation scenarios, use FluentValidation (needs NuGet package):

```bash
dotnet add package FluentValidation
```

```csharp
using FluentValidation;

public record ImagingOrder
{
    public string OrderId { get; init; }
    public string PatientHN { get; init; }
    public string Modality { get; init; }
    public string BodyPart { get; init; }
    public DateTime OrderedDate { get; init; }
    public bool IsUrgent { get; init; }
}

public class ImagingOrderValidator : AbstractValidator<ImagingOrder>
{
    public ImagingOrderValidator()
    {
        RuleFor(x => x.OrderId)
            .NotEmpty()
            .Length(8, 15)
            .WithMessage("Order ID must be 8-15 characters");
        
        RuleFor(x => x.PatientHN)
            .NotEmpty()
            .Matches(@"^[A-Z]{2}\d{6}$")
            .WithMessage("Invalid HN format");
        
        RuleFor(x => x.Modality)
            .Must(m => new[] { "CT", "MRI", "XR", "US", "NM" }.Contains(m))
            .WithMessage("Invalid modality");
        
        RuleFor(x => x.OrderedDate)
            .LessThanOrEqualTo(DateTime.Now)
            .WithMessage("Order date cannot be in the future");
        
        // Conditional validation
        When(x => x.IsUrgent, () =>
        {
            RuleFor(x => x.OrderedDate)
                .Must(date => (DateTime.Now - date).TotalHours <= 24)
                .WithMessage("Urgent orders must be placed within 24 hours");
        });
        
        // Complex cross-property validation
        RuleFor(x => x.BodyPart)
            .NotEmpty()
            .Must((order, bodyPart) => ValidateModalityBodyPartCombination(order.Modality, bodyPart))
            .WithMessage("Invalid modality-body part combination");
    }
    
    private bool ValidateModalityBodyPartCombination(string modality, string bodyPart)
    {
        // Custom business logic
        if (modality == "NM" && bodyPart == "Chest")
            return false; // Example: Nuclear Medicine typically doesn't scan chest alone
        return true;
    }
}

// Usage
var order = new ImagingOrder
{
    OrderId = "ORD123456",
    PatientHN = "RM123456",
    Modality = "CT",
    BodyPart = "Chest",
    OrderedDate = DateTime.Now.AddDays(-1),
    IsUrgent = false
};

var validator = new ImagingOrderValidator();
var validationResult = validator.Validate(order);

if (!validationResult.IsValid)
{
    foreach (var error in validationResult.Errors)
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"Property: {error.PropertyName}");
        Console.WriteLine($"Error: {error.ErrorMessage}");
    }
}
```


## Factory Pattern with Result Type (Production Recommendation)


Instead of throwing exceptions, return validation results - better for business logic:

```csharp
// Result type for validation
public record ValidationResult
{
    public bool IsSuccess { get; init; }
    public List<string> Errors { get; init; } = new();
    
    public static ValidationResult Success() => new() { IsSuccess = true };
    public static ValidationResult Failure(params string[] errors) => 
        new() { IsSuccess = false, Errors = errors.ToList() };
}

public record Result<T>
{
    public bool IsSuccess { get; init; }
    public T? Value { get; init; }
    public List<string> Errors { get; init; } = new();
    
    public static Result<T> Success(T value) => 
        new() { IsSuccess = true, Value = value };
    
    public static Result<T> Failure(params string[] errors) => 
        new() { IsSuccess = false, Errors = errors.ToList() };
}

// Record with private constructor + factory method
public record DicomImage
{
    public string SopInstanceUID { get; init; }
    public int Rows { get; init; }
    public int Columns { get; init; }
    public string TransferSyntax { get; init; }
    
    // Private constructor - force use of factory method
    private DicomImage() { }
    
    // Factory method with validation
    public static Result<DicomImage> Create(
        string sopInstanceUID,
        int rows,
        int columns,
        string transferSyntax)
    {
        var errors = new List<string>();
        
        if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(sopInstanceUID))
            errors.Add("SOP Instance UID cannot be empty");
        
        if (rows <= 0 || rows > 10000)
            errors.Add("Rows must be between 1 and 10000");
        
        if (columns <= 0 || columns > 10000)
            errors.Add("Columns must be between 1 and 10000");
        
        if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(transferSyntax))
            errors.Add("Transfer syntax cannot be empty");
        
        if (errors.Any())
            return Result<DicomImage>.Failure(errors.ToArray());
        
        return Result<DicomImage>.Success(new DicomImage
        {
            SopInstanceUID = sopInstanceUID,
            Rows = rows,
            Columns = columns,
            TransferSyntax = transferSyntax
        });
    }
}

// Usage - no exceptions!
var result = DicomImage.Create(
    sopInstanceUID: "1.2.840.113619.2.55.3.123456.789",
    rows: 512,
    columns: 512,
    transferSyntax: "1.2.840.10008.1.2.1"
);

if (result.IsSuccess)
{
    var image = result.Value;
    Console.WriteLine($"Created DICOM image: {image.Rows}x{image.Columns}");
}
else
{
    Console.WriteLine("Validation failed:");
    result.Errors.ForEach(e => Console.WriteLine($"  - {e}"));
}
```


## Comparison: When to Use Each Approach


```
┌────────────────────┬──────────────┬────────────────┬─────────────────┐
│ Approach           │ Complexity   │ Best For       │ Exception-based │
├────────────────────┼──────────────┼────────────────┼─────────────────┤
│ Constructor        │ Low          │ Simple types   │ Yes             │
│ Validation         │              │ Quick checks   │                 │
├────────────────────┼──────────────┼────────────────┼─────────────────┤
│ Init Accessors     │ Medium       │ Per-property   │ Yes             │
│                    │              │ validation     │                 │
├────────────────────┼──────────────┼────────────────┼─────────────────┤
│ Data Annotations   │ Low-Medium   │ ASP.NET apps   │ No (manual)     │
│                    │              │ DTOs, Models   │                 │
├────────────────────┼──────────────┼────────────────┼─────────────────┤
│ FluentValidation   │ High         │ Complex rules  │ No              │
│                    │              │ Reusable logic │                 │
├────────────────────┼──────────────┼────────────────┼─────────────────┤
│ Factory Pattern    │ Medium-High  │ Domain models  │ No              │
│                    │              │ Business logic │                 │
└────────────────────┴──────────────┴────────────────┴─────────────────┘
```



For your radiology/DICOM work, I'd suggest a **hybrid approach**:

1. **Simple records** (DTOs, API models): Use **Data Annotations**
2. **Domain models** (core business objects): Use **Factory Pattern with Result type**
3. **Complex validation**: Consider **FluentValidation**
